# Practice

The cello started in October, which was fitting, because at first it sounded like something dying.

I don't mean that cruelly. It's just what a cello does in the wrong hands — the bow catching, skidding, the open strings groaning like a door in an old house. Whoever lived on the other side of my bedroom wall practiced at seven every evening for exactly forty minutes. I know it was exactly forty minutes because I had nothing else against which to measure my nights.

I'd come to the city in September, after my mother died and the house went to the bank and everything I owned fit, with room to spare, in a van I returned by five. My furniture was a mattress, a folding table, two chairs inherited from a job that had laid me off. For three weeks I ate standing at the counter and slept facing the wall, and when the sawing began I lay there listening the way you listen to a storm — grateful, almost, that at least something was happening.

Scales first. Up and down, the same eight notes. Then whatever piece they were learning, which stumbled at the same measure every night — so far, stall, back up, stall again. I came to know that measure like a scar. I'd be washing a dish or pretending to read and feel it coming, eight bars of progress and then the wreck, and I'd think: there it is, there's your wall. I never rooted against them. That's the thing I want to be clear about. The sound was terrible and it was the closest thing I had to company.

By December the piece had a shape. I recognized it one night the way you recognize a face across a parking lot — the Bach Cello Suites, the first one, the Prelude, that long climbing figure that repeats and repeats, each time a little higher, like someone trying to describe a dream. My mother had a recording of it. She played it on Sunday mornings while she did the crossword, and I mean that she played the same recording for thirty years, the same cellist, the same morning, so that even now when I hear it I smell coffee and newsprint and feel the particular boredom of being ten.

The cellist next door was not that recording. But in January the wreck-measure got passed, once, at eleven minutes past seven, and I actually sat up. "Yes," I said, out loud, to a wall.

Here is what I knew about my neighbor: they practiced seven to seven-forty. They were worse on Mondays, tight and impatient, the bow digging in. Sundays they played longer, sometimes past eight, and slower, as if nobody was waiting for them afterward. They never played in the morning. Once, in February, they stopped mid-scale, and I heard — faintly, through the plaster — laughing, two people laughing, and it startled me so much I put my hand on the wall. Two people. There were two people over there, having some ordinary evening, one of them holding a cello.

You can love someone this way. Nobody tells you that. There's no word for it — the way you can be carried along for months by the sound of a stranger's effort, how their stumbles become as familiar as your own heartbeat. My life was small and quiet and mostly silent, and somewhere in the winter it reorganized itself around those forty minutes. I started cooking again, real meals, timed so the water boiled while they warmed up. I got a plant. I applied for a job I actually wanted and got it, and came home and told the wall about it — seven-oh-five, mid-scale — "I got it," I said, and the scale stumbled. Coincidence, obviously. I chose to take it as applause.

In March I saw a cello case in the hallway by the mailboxes, propped against the wall, scuffed, one clasp held shut with electrical tape. A door opened somewhere down the corridor. I stood there with my mail in my hand, close enough to touch the case, and I made a decision I still think was wise: I left before whoever it was came back. I decided not to know. Some things you keep in the room they came in.

Then, in April, silence.

One day, then two. A week. I told myself people travel, people get sick, people quit hobbies after eight months of making their neighbors miserable. But the apartment had gone back to being exactly what it was before October — a box with me in it — and I discovered, standing in the kitchen at seven holding a colander, listening to nothing, how much I had been leaning on that sound. How much weight it carried without my noticing. I grieved for someone I'd never seen. I stood at the wall and considered knocking and rehearsed what I'd say, which was nothing, because there was nothing to say. *Hello, I'm the person who listens to you* is not a thing you say to a stranger.

Nine days. On the ninth I came home late and it was already going — but wrong. Tentative. The tone gone soft and careful, all the confidence of winter scraped away. Something had happened over there. I never learned what. That's the arrangement; that's the whole arrangement, actually: you get the sound and not the story. I sat on the floor with my back against our shared wall and listened to a stranger start over, and it was the Prelude, from the beginning, slow, like a penance, like a promise — and somewhere in the second minute I understood I was crying, quietly, the way you cry at something that isn't sad.

They got it back. It took weeks, but the wall was passed again, then passed easily, then passed at speed. And then one evening in June it happened: the Prelude, whole, beginning to end, no wreck, no stall, every repetition climbing clean, the entire long architecture of it standing up at last. I sat on the kitchen floor and felt two things at once — pride, and a strange grief — because I knew what came next. That's how practice works. You don't finish. You conquer a thing, and it releases you to something harder.

The next night, at seven, something new began. Unfamiliar, thorny, terrible.

I put water on for pasta and smiled at the wall.

message.reasoning:
The prompt is beautifully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you."

This is an invitation to write something genuine, creative, and interesting. No constraints except the word count. Let me think about what would be worth writing.

Options:
1. A short story
2. An essay/meditation on something
3. Something experimental/meta
4. Something personal-feeling
5. A poem sequence
6. Something that plays with the form itself

The meta-approach (writing about having 1000 words) is tempting but often feels cheap. Let me think about what would actually be compelling.

What comes to me when I sit with this? Let me actually think rather than immediately reaching for a form.

Something about... attention? The way we spend words like currency? No, too meta again.

A short story could work well. What story? Something small and human. Or something strange.

Actually, let me think about what I genuinely find interesting to explore:

- The nature of memory and how it distorts
- Small moments that carry enormous weight
- The strangeness of ordinary things
- Time
- The way people fail to communicate but connect anyway
- Objects that hold histories

One idea: a story about someone who repairs things — a repair shop for objects, but really it's about the people who bring them. A woman bringing in a clock, a man bringing in a radio that hasn't worked in decades. Each repair is really about grief or love or time.

Another idea: something about a lighthouse keeper, or a night shift worker, someone alone with their thoughts in a liminal time.

Another: a piece about hands — all the things hands do, have done. Too listy maybe.

Another: something about the last speaker of a language? Overdone perhaps.

Another: a story told through inventory — the contents of a house being sorted after a death. Each object opening a memory. That's a bit done too but could work if the voice is strong.

Another idea: something about the moment before something happens — the elasticity of time. The second before the phone rings with bad news. The way time behaves.

Another: write about the word itself — words. Hmm, meta again.

Let me try the repair shop idea. A woman who fixes things. People bring her broken objects and she can tell from the way they're broken what happened. A clock stopped at a specific time. A watch worn on the wrong wrist. A music box. The story could be about her, or about one customer.

Or: a story about a message in a bottle, but told from the bottle's perspective? No, too whimsical.

Or something more essayistic — a meditation that moves. Like an essay about silence, or about the specific quality of light at certain hours, that drifts through memory and observation. Lyric essay territory.

Actually, what comes to me most strongly when I sit with "write whatever comes to you" — I think about the strange position of writing itself, of being asked to fill a space with words, and what's worth saying. But instead of being meta about it in a clever way, maybe I can use that as a doorway into something real.

Let me try a hybrid: begin with the writer sitting down, but then let the writing escape into a story or memory or meditation — showing the mind actually moving. That could be honest to the prompt: whatever comes to you. The mind doesn't come to one thing; it comes to several, and the connections between them are the actual subject.

Structure idea:
- Start with the blank space of the page/screen
- A specific image arrives — say, a memory of a specific moment
- Follow it
- Let it connect to something larger
- End somewhere that feels earned

What specific image? Let me invent something vivid. Ideas:
- A father teaching to whittle, the smell of wood
- A grandmother's kitchen, the specific sound of a screen door
- Snow falling under a streetlight
- A dog waiting at a window
- The blue glow of a television in a dark room
- Someone learning to skip stones

Skipping stones — that has built-in metaphorical weight (counting the skips, the effort, the water) but might be cliché.

What about the sound of someone practicing an instrument badly, heard through apartment walls? That's lovely — you hear someone's effort, their failure, their persistence, and you never see them. A stranger becoming familiar through their mistakes. That's a genuinely interesting observation about modern life — intimacy with strangers we never meet.

Story: A person who lives next to (or below, or across from) someone practicing the cello (or violin, or trumpet). Badly at first. Over months, they improve. The narrator never meets them. Then one day the practicing stops. The narrator worries, grieves a relationship that never existed in any legible form. Maybe it resumes. Maybe the neighbor moves away. The story is about all the relationships we have that don't count as relationships — the ones with no name.

That feels true and specific and a little sad and a little hopeful. Let me draft it.

Voice: first person, literary but not overwrought. Present tense or past? Present could give immediacy — "The cello starts at seven."

Actually, let me make it richer: the narrator could be going through something — a loss, a divorce, insomnia, grief — and the cello practice becomes the spine of their days. The improvement of the stranger mirrors or contrasts with the narrator's own stalled life.

Let me think about who the narrator is. Keep it unspecified in gender. They've recently lost someone or something — maybe a partner left, maybe a parent died, maybe they moved to the city after a life elsewhere. Moving to a new city is good — everything is unfamiliar, and the one familiar thing is a stranger's scales.

Draft outline:
1. Opening: the sound begins. Describe the badness of it specifically — the way a beginner cello sounds, the E-string or open strings, sawing.
2. The narrator's situation: newly arrived, or newly alone. The apartment empty.
3. The routine develops: scales at seven, a piece attempted, abandoned, returned to. The narrator learns the stranger's habits through sound — when they're frustrated (louder, more sawing), when they're tired.
4. Progress: over months, the sound changes. A piece emerges recognizably — maybe the Bach Cello Suites, which every cellist practices. The Prelude. That's a good choice — instantly recognizable, famously difficult, gorgeous.
5. A crisis: the sound stops. Days of silence. The narrator realizes they care — that this one-sided intimacy matters.
6. Resolution: it returns, changed — better, or different. Or: the narrator finally sees the cellist by accident and it's not what they imagined — an old man, a kid, someone unexpected. Or they never see them and that's the point. Maybe the ending: the narrator takes up something themselves — answering. Or simply the ending is the narrator listening to the Bach now played all the way through, and crying, or making dinner, and life continuing.

Ending on life continuing quietly feels right. Maybe the final beat: one evening the cellist plays the piece perfectly, and then never plays it again — moves on to harder things, ruining it again, beginning again. And the narrator finds they loved the ruining too. The beginning again. That's the emotional insight: we love people at their beginnings.

That's a good final note. The perfection is not the point; the daily returning is.

Let me also think: should I frame it with the meta idea (being given 1000 words)? I think no — just write the story cleanly. The prompt gives freedom; the best answer is to use it well, not to talk about using it. Maybe a title? A title could be nice: "The Cellist Next Door" is flat. "Scales" — simple, good. "Open Strings" — nice double meaning. "The Wall Between Us" — too romance-y. "Adagio"? "Practice" — I like "Practice." It carries the theme: practice as repetition, as ritual, as something you never finish.

Word count: I should aim for around 1000 words since that was the frame given. The user said "You have 1000 words" — I should honor that, roughly. Something close to 1000, maybe 900-1000. Let me write with that target and keep an eye on it.

Months pass. Improvement. Identify the piece: the Bach Prelude, Suite No. 1. The narrator's own life improves in parallel — small things: a job, plants, they start cooking actual meals timed to the forty minutes. The neighbor's practice becomes clock, companion, ritual.

And under that, grief — the mother's death, the displacement — softened by a stranger's scales.

Should the narrator ever see the cellist? I think no — or almost: maybe once, a glimpse that's inconclusive, someone carrying a case in the hall, but they can't be sure, and they choose not to find out. Choosing not to know is a nice beat — preserving the relationship exactly as it is.

Actually, maybe better: they see a cello case in the hallway/mailroom once and deliberately don't look at the name/face. "I decided not to know." That's a strong small moment.

Let me write the full thing now, keeping it near 1000 words. I'll write in a natural literary register, first person, past tense with present-tense frame? Simple past throughout, told retrospectively. Keep sentences varied. Avoid purple prose but allow a few images to shine.

**Practice**

The cello started in October, which was fitting, because at first it sounded like something dying.

I don't mean that cruelly. It's just what a cello does in the wrong hands — the bow catching, skidding, the open strings groaning like a door in an old house. Whoever lived on the other side of my bedroom wall practiced at seven every evening for exactly forty minutes. I know it was exactly forty minutes because I had nothing else against which to measure my nights.

I'd come to the city in September, after my mother died and the house went to the bank and everything I owned fit, with room to spare, in a van I returned by five. My furniture was a mattress, a folding table, two chairs inherited from a job that had laid me off. For three weeks I ate standing at the counter and slept facing the wall, and when the sawing began I lay there listening the way you listen to a storm — grateful, almost, that at least something was happening.

Scales first. Up and down, the same eight notes. Then whatever piece they were learning, which stumbled at the same measure every night — so far, stall, back up, stall again. I came to know that measure like a scar. I'd be washing a dish or pretending to read and feel it coming, eight bars of progress and then the wreck, and I'd think: there it is, there's your wall. I never rooted against them. That's the thing I want to be clear about. The sound was terrible and it was the closest thing I had to company.

By December the piece had a shape. I recognized it one night the way you recognize a face across a parking lot — the Bach Cello Suites, the first one, the Prelude, that long climbing figure that repeats and repeats, each time a little higher, like someone trying to describe a dream. My mother had a recording of it. She played it on Sunday mornings while she did the crossword, and I mean that she played the same recording for thirty years, the same cellist, the same morning, so that even now when I hear it I smell coffee and newsprint and feel the particular boredom of being ten.

The cellist next door was not that recording. But in January the wreck-measure got passed, once, at eleven minutes past seven, and I actually sat up. "Yes," I said, out loud, to a wall.

Here is what I knew about my neighbor: they practiced seven to seven-forty. They were worse on Mondays, tight and impatient, the bow digging in. Sundays they played longer, past eight sometimes, and slower, as if nobody was waiting for them afterward. They never played in the morning. Once, in February, they stopped mid-scale, and I heard — faintly, through the wall — laughing, two people laughing, and it startled me so much I put my hand on the plaster. Two people. There were two people over there, having some ordinary evening, one of them holding a cello.

You can love someone this way. Nobody tells you that. There's no word for it — the way you can be carried along for months by the sound of a stranger's effort, how their stumbles become as familiar as your own heartbeat. My life was small and quiet and mostly silent, and somewhere in the winter it reorganized itself around those forty minutes. I started cooking again, real meals, timed so the water boiled while they warmed up. I got a plant. I applied for a job I actually wanted and got it and came home and told the wall about it, seven-oh-five, mid-scale, "I got it," I said, and the scale stumbled — coincidence, obviously, but I chose to take it as applause.

In March I saw a cello case in the hallway by the mailboxes, propped against the wall, scuffed, one clasp held shut with electrical tape. A door opened somewhere down the corridor. I stood there with my mail in my hand, close enough to touch the case, and I made a decision I still think was wise: I left before whoever it was came back. I decided not to know. Some things you keep in the room they came in.

Then in April, silence.

One day, then two. A week. I told myself people travel, people get sick, people lose interest after eight months of a hobby that makes their neighbors hate them. But the apartment had gone back to being exactly what it had been before October, a box with me in it, and I discovered — standing in the kitchen at seven, holding a colander, listening to nothing — how much I had been leaning on that sound. How much weight it had been carrying without my noticing. I grieved for someone I'd never seen. I stood at the wall and considered knocking and rehearsed what I'd say, which was nothing, there was nothing to say, hello, I'm the person who listens to you, that's not a thing you say to a stranger.

Nine days. On the ninth day I came home late and it was already going — but wrong, tentative, the tone gone soft and careful, all the confidence of winter scraped away. Something had happened over there. I never learned what. That's the arrangement; that's the whole arrangement, actually: you get the sound and not the story. I sat on the floor with my back against our shared wall and listened to a stranger start over, and it was the Prelude, from the beginning, slow, like a penance, like an apology, like a promise — and somewhere in the second minute I understood I was crying, quietly, the way you cry at something that isn't sad.

They got it back. It took weeks, but the wall was passed again, then passed easily, then passed at speed. And then one evening in June it happened: the Prelude, whole, beginning to end, no wreck, no stall, every repetition climbing clean, the whole long architecture of it standing up at last — and I sat there on the kitchen floor and felt two things at once, pride and a strange grief, because I knew what came next. That's how practice works. You don't finish. You conquer a thing and it releases you to something harder.

The next night, at seven, something new began — unfamiliar, thorny, terrible. I put water on for pasta and smiled at the wall.
